question_name: Compressed or packed reference-image re-scan of already-pulled dumps
findings: A byte-level re-scan of all seven listed files for compression magic bytes (gzip 1f 8b, xz fd 37 7a 58 5a 00, lz4 04 22 4d 18 / legacy 02 21 4c 18, zstd 28 b5 2f fd, bzip2 42 5a 68) and archive signatures (cpio 070701/070702, tar 'ustar', ext4 superblock magic 0xEF53 at candidate-offset+1080) found: (1) uboot.bin -- 2 raw gzip-magic byte pairs (offsets 0x518c and 0x20518c), both failed real gzip decompression (GzipFile raised on the very first read) -- coincidental 2-byte matches, not real streams. 2 ext4-magic byte occurrences, neither had a plausible superblock (inodes_count/blocks_count/log_block_size out of sane range) at magic_offset-1080. No cpio/tar/lz4/zstd/bzip2 hits at all. (2) trust.bin -- zero hits of any kind for any magic. (3) pre_gpt_pre_reboot.bin -- zero compression/archive hits; 15 raw 0xEF53 byte occurrences, none forming a plausible ext4 superblock. (post_reboot copy skipped per instructions, confirmed identical file size/name pattern to pre copy.) (4) boot_orig.img -- 117 raw gzip-magic hits (all coincidental, 0 decompressed), 5 cpio-header hits (these are the already-known plaintext ramdisk cpio structure concatenated into the boot image -- not new), 140 ext4-magic occurrences (0 plausible superblocks), and exactly ONE real, fully valid xz stream at absolute offset 16,410,053 (0xFA65C5). It decompresses cleanly (lzma.FORMAT_XZ, no errors, full end-of-stream marker present) to 25,978,880 bytes. Extracting it with Python's tarfile module confirms it IS a valid uncompressed POSIX/GNU-ustar tar archive (8,770 members, all with ustar magic 'ustar\x00' and uname='txcz', 512-byte-header-aligned -- this is what produced the 8,770 raw 'ustar' string hits inside the decompressed buffer, all real, not coincidental). Its member list is exclusively a Linux kernel header tree (./include/uapi/rdma/*, ./include/uapi/gpu/arm/bifrost/* Mali driver headers, ./arch/*, etc.) -- i.e. this is the kernel's own CONFIG_IKHEADERS feature (normally exposed at runtime as /sys/kernel/kheaders.tar.xz), embedded in the kernel image purely so out-of-tree kernel modules can be built against the running kernel's exact headers. Zero members reference /system, and there is no init.rc file anywhere in the archive (checked both by exact name and substring). This is a well-documented, completely standard, benign kernel feature -- not a golden /system or init.rc reference. (5) ramdisk_orig.cpio -- confirmed it is the known cpio (14 real header hits, matches its own structure, not re-flagged as a finding per instructions). It also contains 1 real xz stream (offset 0x23eaba) decompressing to a 765,496-byte ARM32 ELF whose string table is full of bionic/android::init C++ symbols (SwitchRoot, RebootSystem, StartConsole, fs_mgr_overlayfs_filesystem_available, hashtree_info::initialize, etc.) -- explained below, this is the same artifact as in init_extracted.bin (ramdisk_orig.cpio contains init_extracted.bin as a member, so the same bytes appear in both files). (6) init_extracted.bin -- 1 real xz stream at offset 0x23df6a, same 765,496-byte ARM32 ELF as above. Inspecting the 40 bytes immediately preceding the xz magic in the OUTER file shows the ASCII section-name strings '...rodata\0.gnu_debugdata\0.data\0' directly abutting the xz magic bytes. This is the standard GNU/glibc-toolchain '.gnu_debugdata' ELF section (aka MiniDebugInfo): objcopy/strip compress a stripped-down ELF containing only the minimal symbol table into an xz blob stored as a normal ELF section, specifically so a small production binary keeps just enough symbol info for backtraces/debugging without shipping full debug info. The decompressed 765KB ELF sharing the outer binary's own architecture (ei_class=1/32-bit, e_machine=40/ARM, matching init_extracted.bin's own header) and containing init's own mangled symbol names is exactly what MiniDebugInfo looks like -- it is a symbol table for THIS SAME BINARY, not a second executable and not a filesystem reference. (7) super_header.bin -- 108 raw gzip-magic hits (0 decompressed), 80 ext4-magic occurrences (0 plausible superblocks), 18 real xz streams at 18 distinct offsets, EVERY one immediately preceded by the identical '...rodata\0.gnu_debugdata\0.data\0' ELF-shstrtab pattern, each decompressing to a distinct small-to-medium ARM ELF (sizes ranging 188 bytes to 356,620 bytes). These are MiniDebugInfo sections belonging to several different stripped ELF binaries/shared-objects whose raw bytes happen to fall within the 16MB address range this dump covers -- meaning this 'liblp metadata dump' region physically contains real compiled-binary content (not just liblp header+geometry+partition-table padding as its label implies), but still no filesystem image, no init.rc, and no /system reference of any kind. No lz4 or zstd magic bytes (raw or otherwise) were found in any of the seven files, so there is nothing to flag as 'found but unextractable without a new dependency.' No bzip2 magic was found anywhere. No tar 'ustar' signature was found directly in any raw (undecompressed) file region -- the only 'ustar' occurrences exist inside the one already-explained decompressed kernel-headers tarball. No ext4 superblock candidate across any file, in any file, at any offset, passed the plausibility check (sane inodes_count / blocks_count / log_block_size at magic_offset-1080).
relevance_to_our_symptoms: This fails to explain the observed whole-partition /system repopulation. Every compression/archive signature that turned out to be a real, successfully-decompressed stream was identified and explained as a completely standard, benign toolchain artifact: (a) the Linux kernel's own CONFIG_IKHEADERS embedded headers.tar.xz inside boot_orig.img, and (b) '.gnu_debugdata' MiniDebugInfo ELF sections (a symbol table for the SAME binary, standard objcopy/strip output) found inside init_extracted.bin, ramdisk_orig.cpio (because it contains init_extracted.bin), and scattered through super_header.bin's slack space. None of these seven files contain init.rc content, a /system reference, or an ext4 filesystem image anywhere -- compressed, packed, or otherwise. This closes off the 'packed reference is hiding in one of these already-pulled dumps' hypothesis for all files checked so far; the restore mechanism's reference data (if it exists as static data at all, rather than being generated/fetched some other way) must live somewhere NOT yet pulled and scanned -- most likely inside the actual compiled boot_android/android_bootloader logic in uboot.bin itself (as a hardcoded MMC/eMMC LBA offset it reads from directly, rather than as a self-contained blob within these dump files), or on a partition that hasn't been dumped and scanned this way yet (e.g. the real `system`/`super` partition itself only ever gets grep'd for plaintext per the outline, never magic-byte/decompression-scanned the way this task did for the boot-chain files).
confidence: high for the negative result on all seven files (byte-exact stdlib magic-byte scan plus successful full decompression via Python's own gzip/lzma/bz2 modules is deterministic, not heuristic) and high for the two 'benign artifact' explanations specifically (CONFIG_IKHEADERS and .gnu_debugdata are both independently verifiable, well-documented public formats, and the on-disk byte context -- literal ELF section-name strings immediately preceding each xz magic -- directly confirms the .gnu_debugdata identification without needing external lookup). Medium confidence only on one narrower point: whether super_header.bin's 16MB region containing real ELF binary data (beyond liblp metadata) is itself meaningful/suspicious -- it is left as an open observation rather than further chased here, since it does not contain an init.rc or filesystem reference either way.
sources_or_method: Custom Python 3 script (stdlib only: gzip, lzma, bz2, tarfile, struct, re -- no third-party packages) reading each file fully into memory and (1) enumerating every offset of each magic-byte pattern via bytes.find() in a loop, (2) for gzip/xz/bzip2 hits, attempting real decompression via GzipFile/lzma.decompress(FORMAT_XZ)/bz2.decompress at that exact offset and recording success/failure plus decompressed content, (3) for cpio/tar hits, recording raw offsets and (for tar) checking 512-byte header alignment, (4) for the 0xEF53 ext4-magic pattern, computing candidate_fs_start = magic_offset-1080 and validating inodes_count/blocks_count_lo/log_block_size fields at that computed superblock start for plausibility. Follow-up manual analysis: tarfile.open() on the boot_orig.img decompressed buffer to enumerate real tar members; struct-based ELF header parsing (ei_class/ei_data/e_type/e_machine) and raw hex-context inspection immediately preceding each xz magic to identify the .gnu_debugdata pattern. Limitation: lz4 and zstd are NOT in the Python standard library (would require the third-party lz4 or zstandard/python-zstd packages) -- moot here since zero raw magic-byte matches for either format were found in any of the seven files, so no extraction was skipped due to missing tooling. Limitation: the ext4-superblock plausibility check is a heuristic (range-sanity on 3 fields), not a full checksum/structure validation, so it could in principle reject a genuine but unusual superblock -- mitigated by the fact that zero candidates even had the right byte pattern in a remotely sane location to begin with.
safe_next_step: Since the packed-blob hypothesis is now exhausted for every file already pulled, the next zero-risk step is to re-target the STATIC DISASSEMBLY item (already in this outline) specifically at finding a hardcoded raw MMC/eMMC block-offset or LBA constant inside uboot.bin's boot_android/android_bootloader machine code -- i.e. look for the reference data being read directly from a fixed sector range on the eMMC via mmc_bread/blk_dread-style calls, rather than being unpacked from a self-contained compressed blob living inside uboot.bin, trust.bin, or the boot image. If such an offset constant is found in the disassembly, the safe follow-up is to compute that absolute eMMC byte offset and, if a full raw eMMC image (not just the individual named-partition dumps already collected) is ever available locally, magic-byte/decompression-scan specifically at that offset using the exact same method as this task, rather than re-scanning the same seven already-cleared files. Also worth a quick incidental follow-up: since super_header.bin's later region contains real stripped-binary bytes with MiniDebugInfo (not just liblp padding), a plaintext string pass over super_header.bin's tail (beyond wherever the real liblp header+table ends) might reveal which partition/build that spillover content actually belongs to, purely as a labeling/provenance clarification -- low priority, does not bear directly on the /system-restore mechanism.
risky_next_step_if_pursued: If disassembly and further local dumps genuinely exhaust the safe options, the only way to be fully certain no packed reference exists ANYWHERE on the eMMC would be to pull a complete raw eMMC image (every LBA, not just named partitions) and repeat this same magic-byte/decompression scan across the entire device, which requires read access to the physical device (e.g. via a working ADB/fastboot/recovery shell with `dd` access to /dev/block/mmcblkX, or a full eMMC-to-image dump via Maskrom/EDL-style hardware programming). This is explicitly device interaction, which this task's constraints and the project's own safety posture rule out performing here; even a read-only full-device dump carries real risk on this hardware given the user's already-documented finding that Maskrom recovery requires hardware access this project treats as its real practical blocker -- an interrupted or misconfigured dump attempt on a device with unknown eMMC command quirks is not risk-free.
risk_level: low for the dump-and-scan itself if it could be done read-only (no writes), but the enabling precondition -- getting a full raw eMMC image off this specific device at all -- is gated behind the project's already-identified hardware-access blocker (Maskrom needs physical access), so in practice this next step is currently unreachable rather than merely risky.
